description.narrative: Inter-ministerial cooperation strengthened in the area of data collection on work-related injuries. In 2020 – 2021, research has been commissioned by the Government, and involving several institutions, to collect and analyse occupational injuries in the country, both fatal and non-fatal. Not only is this is the most comprehensive data available on the subject in Qatar, but the exercise also identified the various gaps that exist in OSH data collection, with a view to working collectively to address them. The ILO-ADLSA technical cooperation project funded the Unified Registry of Work-Related Injuries in Qatar (WURQ), through the Hamad Medical Research Centre. This research grant led to the collection of data in 2020. The ILO also participated in several meetings with ADLSA, MOPH, Hamad, etc. to discuss the monthly figures, and identify how data collection could be further strengthened. The ILO prepared a report for publication on how data on occupational injuries in Qatar is collected, analysed and used.

description.narrative:
Labour inspection strategy adopted and implemented by the Ministry of Administrative Development, Labour and Social Affairs (ADLSA) in 2020. The strategy is aligned with national priorities and the commitments stemming from the ratification of ILO Convention 81. It reaffirms the role and functions of the labour inspectorate particularly in light of the ongoing labour reform agenda in the country. It calls for the use of strategic and consistent approaches to labour inspection. The aims and content of the Policy have been communicated to all labour inspectors in the country, as part of a training programme. In line with the goals of the strategy, more detailed reports have been prepared on labour inspection activities.
National Action Plan on human trafficking and forced labour adopted. The National Action Plan on human trafficking was expanded to incorporate elements on forced labour in 2020. The activities carried out by the National Committee on Combatting Human Trafficking (NCCHT) reflect this broader scope, with training for member institutions, the drafting of a gap analysis on Protocol 29 on Forced Labour, awareness raising activities and the publication of a Handbook on Trafficking and Forced Labour.
In January 2020, the State of Qatar adopted Ministerial Decision No. 95 of 2019 that removed the requirement for migrant workers, including domestic workers, to receive an exit permit to leave the country anytime, temporarily or permanently, during their contract. Extending the coverage of Law No. 13 of 2018, the Ministerial Decision applies to workers who are not prescribed by the Labour Law. These categories of workers include domestic workers, workers in ministries and other government entities, workers in public institutions, workers employed at sea, workers in agriculture, and workers employed in casual work. As per the adopted legislation, domestic workers have to inform their employers, verbally or in writing, at least 72 hours before they depart. The strategy was developed with inputs from the ILO, following consultations with ADLSA on the need to adopt more strategic approaches to labour inspection, and on the importance of data collection and analysis, cooperation with other ministries and reporting. The strategy was promoted among labour inspectors in a training course that was developed with the International Training Centre (ITC-ILO Turin).
The ILO provided support to the main activities on the NCCHT, including organizing training together with the UK Embassy in Qatar; the preparation of the Handbook; the drafting of the gap analysis; and the production of a short video with several embassies to mark the World Day against Trafficking.
The ILO provided inputs to the drafting of the legislation. In addition, the ILO developed various communication materials to increase awareness of the Ministerial Decision including FAQs, infographics and an animation video.
The ILO-ADLSA technical cooperation programme conducted a study to inform policy reforms related migrant workers ability to change employers. The study assessed the economic impact of increased labour market mobility on enterprises while capturing workers' perspectives on reform options. The ILO and ADLSA convened a workshop in March 2019 to present the preliminary findings of the study to national stakeholders. The ILO subsequently provided inputs during the drafting of the legislation. Upon adoption of the legislation, the ILO supported the development of communication materials to increase awareness including FAQs, infographics and an animation video.

description.narrative:
Law and Ministerial Decision on minimum wage adopted in September 2020, establishing a non-discriminatory minimum wage that came into force in March 2021. The Law applies to all workers, of all nationalities and sectors, including domestic workers. The Law establish a minimum basic wage, as well as minimum thresholds for food and accommodation. It is the first such legislation in the region. Over 251,000 workers saw their basic salaries increase since the Law came into force.
Minimum Wage Commission was established by Law, with the mandate to review the impact of the minimum wage, and propose adjustments. The Minimum Wage Commission has already been formed with representation from several ministries. The Commission will also consult with workers, employers and experts. The ILO-Ministry of Administrative Development, Labour and Social Affairs (ADLSA) technical cooperation project conducted a study on wages in the country, and the cost of living – both for workers in Qatar as well as their family members back home. The study proposed different thresholds and the impact on labour costs. The ILO participated in consultations, including among different institutions. The ILO provided information that shaped in the legislation, including the key principles from Convention 131 on minimum wage fixing.
The establishment of a body similar to that of a minimum wage commission is one of the principles of ILO Convention 131 on minimum wage fixing. In addition to promoting this as a necessary part of the law, the ILO shared good practices on the formulation of minimum wage commissions from other countries.

description.narrative:
National OSH policy adopted by Ministry of Administrative Development, Labour and Social Affairs (ADLSA) and the Ministry of Public Health (MOPH), in October 2020. The joint policy is the first of its kind and was developed following a series of consultations among a number of government and non-government entities, and consultations with employers and workers. The policy focuses on prevention, with five mains areas of action: 1) coordination, cooperation and consultation mechanisms; 2) data collection and analysis; 3) legislation; 4) provision of health services; and 5) education and training. It provides a common framework from which to launch strategic OSH interventions in the country.
Heat stress legislation was adopted in May 2021, and guidance was also issued to employers and workers to ensure understanding and compliance with the new legislation. Ministerial Decision 15 of 2021 extended the prohibited hours for outdoor work, introduced a maximum Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) threshold, and called on employers to provide workers with annual health checks, among other prevention measures. The guidance took the form of an online resource book, as well as short FAQs and animations, developed in multiple languages. The legislation is evidence-based, drawing on research carried out in 2019. It is the most specific national legislation known to exist on heat stress. The ILO was involved in the consultations on the OSH policy from the start, providing guidance on the content and the process. The ILO also helped ADLSA to organize consultations with workers and employers. The ILO has also supported ADLSA-MOPH to cooperate on activities, that has been borne out of this Policy.
The ILO provided inputs to the draft legislation as well as the guidance tools. The ILO has supported the translation and distribution of the guidance materials through Social Media, and ILO & ADLSA website. The 2019 research that informed the legislation was commissioned as part of the ILO-ADLSA development cooperation programme.
